title: How I Read a 30-Second Commercial Script (Voiceover Breakdown)
creator: Jules Okafor
description:
A full commercial read, start to finish, and then everything I was thinking while I did it: where the breaths go, which word gets the smile, and why the call to action is the hardest line in the script.

The practice script in this video is one I wrote myself. Driftwell is not a real company, please don't go looking for the mattress.

New voiceover tips every Tuesday.

00:00 Why commercial reads are hard
01:05 The practice read
01:40 The breakdown
04:10 Homework

Gear: an old dynamic mic, a closet full of coats, and a lot of patience.

sentences.t: Hey, it's Jules, welcome back to the booth, which is, yes, still my closet.
So a lot of you asked after the audiobook video, okay, but how do you do commercials, because that's where the money is, right?
And, yeah, kind of, but commercial reads are weirdly the hardest thing to sound natural on, because the copy is written by somebody who has never had to say it out loud.
You get thirty seconds, you get maybe seventy words, and every single one of them has been fought over in a meeting.
So today I'm going to do a full read of a practice script, and then we're going to tear it apart line by line.
I wrote this one myself, it's for a mattress company that does not exist, so please don't email me asking where to buy it.
Okay, slating it, take one, Driftwell, thirty seconds.
Tired of waking up more tired than when you went to bed?
Meet Driftwell, the mattress that keeps you cool, quiet, and comfortable all night long.
With three layers of cooling foam and a hundred night trial, you can sleep on it, love it, or send it back.
Free delivery, no hassle, no pushy salespeople.
Head to driftwell dot com and use code DREAMDEEP for twenty percent off your first order.
Driftwell, finally, a better morning.
Okay.
So that came in at twenty nine and a half seconds, which is good, you always want a little room for the music to land at the end.
Let's start with that opening question, because that is the line that gets most people.
The temptation is to go big, like, TIRED of waking up, and that's how you sound like a late night infomercial from nineteen ninety eight.
What I'm actually doing is talking to one person who is sitting on the edge of their bed at six in the morning, and I'm a little sympathetic, like, yeah, me too.
Then the brand name, that's the one word in the whole script the client actually cares about, so it gets a tiny lift and a smile, but just a tiny one.
If you hit the brand name too hard it sounds like you're being paid to say it, which, you are, but they don't want to hear that.
The features line is a list, and lists are a trap, because people read them like a grocery list, flat, flat, flat.
I give each item its own little picture, cool is a feeling, quiet is a feeling, comfortable is where I land and kind of relax.
Now, the line every voice actor dreads, the call to action, the web address and the code.
This is where the copywriter crammed in everything legal and marketing wanted, and you have about four seconds to say it without sounding like a robot or an auctioneer.
My trick is I slow down on the address, because people actually have to remember it, and I let the discount ride on a smile so it sounds like a little gift and not a disclaimer.
And watch your sibilance on lines like that, because a lot of esses in a row on a cheap mic will spike and the engineer will hate you.
Last line is the tag, and the tag is a landing, not a launch.
You've been selling for twenty eight seconds, now you just put it down gently, like you're closing a door in a house where a baby is asleep.
Okay, homework.
Grab any ad you heard this week, on the radio, on a podcast, whatever, write it down word for word, and read it to one specific person in your head.
Record it twice, once trying to sell, once just talking, and I promise the second one will be the one you'd book.
Send me your takes in the comments, I read all of them, and next Tuesday we're doing video game character auditions, which is a completely different kind of chaos.
See you in the closet.
